bushfireheat

bushfireheat helps risk analysts who price bushfire exposure in south-eastern Australia answer one question: how much more often does extreme heat occur in the fire season now than in 1950–1979, and does the answer depend on where the threshold for “extreme” is set?

The package contains daily fire-season weather for eight towns affected by the 2019/20 Black Summer fires, functions that count hot days and compare periods, and a Shiny app for exploring the change town by town.

Documentation website: https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-hanwen-l/

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-hanwen-l")

Launch the app 

library(bushfireheat)
run_app()

Use the functions 

seasons <- summarise_seasons(fire_daily, threshold = 35)
compare_periods(seasons)
plot_hot_days(seasons)

Data

fire_daily holds the daily maximum temperature and rainfall for every day of every September–February fire season from 1950/51 to 2025/26, and fire_towns lists the towns. The values come from the ERA5 reanalysis (Hersbach et al. 2023, https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.adbb2d47), retrieved through the Open-Meteo Historical Weather API under the CC BY 4.0 licence. Generated using Copernicus Climate Change Service information. The daily values were subset to fire-season months; no other changes were made.

data-raw/fire_daily.R downloads and prepares the data. Raw downloads are cached in data-raw/raw/, so the script rebuilds the package data without calling the API again.

Generative AI declaration

Generative AI declaration: I used Claude (Claude Code, Anthropic) to explain the assignment requirements, compare candidate data sources and test the Open-Meteo API, and to draft the initial package structure: the data-preparation script, the exported functions with their documentation and tests, a starter Shiny app, this README and the vignette. I checked and revised all generated code and text.
